item_text: **Prenominal disease names.** A multiword disease name, or an abbreviation whose expansion names a disease defined earlier in the text, that directly precedes a head noun is annotated as **Modifier**, provided the span is not coordinated (Section 2). The head noun and any following nomenclature tokens are left unannotated. This applies whether the head denotes a clinical or population entity (e.g., “ovarian cancer cases,” “fragile X syndrome patients”) or a gene, protein, or gene symbol (e.g., “ancient SLS genes,” where “SLS” is defined earlier in the abstract; “breast cancer susceptibility gene 1,” where “breast cancer” is the Modifier and “susceptibility gene 1” is not annotated). Do not infer that the disease span is O merely because the whole noun phrase names a gene or protein. Adjectival forms such as “G6PD deficient phenotype” are also **Modifiers** (see Section 1, rule B(i)). Deficit-named disorders used prenominally (e.g., “C7 deficiency patients”) are likewise **Modifiers**.

item_text: - If the disease-denoting span is itself the nominal head of its noun phrase, including when that noun phrase is the complement of a preposition such as “of” or “with,” or is a clausal subject or object that refers to the disease as an entity, label the span **Specific Disease**. A preceding frame noun (e.g., “history,” “risk,” “patients”) does not make the span a Modifier when the disease is the head of its own phrase. Examples: “family history of ovarian cancer” (the disease heads the “of”-complement) and “risk of ovarian cancer” are **Specific Disease**; “ovarian cancer risk” (the disease precedes a non-disease head) is **Modifier**.

item_text: A disease span whose head is an unqualified generic category noun, a superordinate term naming a class of conditions rather than one named condition, is labeled **Disease Class**. This holds even when the span sits in a prepositional or clausal frame that elsewhere hosts Specific Diseases (e.g., “associated with ___,” “characterized by ___”), unless the *Reference-frame precedence* rule above applies. Otherwise, lexical specificity, not the governing frame, decides the type. A clinical-state anchor under clause (a) does not change this, because the anchor fixes a subject, not a single named condition.
